Class NetworkAddressPolicy

Namespace

Decides whether an outbound connection may reach an address: the building block against server-side request forgery (SSRF) when an application fetches a URL somebody else supplied.

Remarks

The decision is taken on the IP address, never on the text of the URL. A host name proves nothing about where it resolves — a public domain can carry an A record of 10.0.0.5, and can change it between a check and the connection (DNS rebinding). Pair this policy with PublicNetworkConnector, which applies it to the address a socket actually connects to.

By default only publicly routable unicast addresses are allowed. Denied: loopback, private (RFC 1918 and IPv6 unique-local), link-local (which includes the cloud instance metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254), carrier-grade NAT, documentation and benchmarking ranges, multicast, reserved space, the IPv6 transition prefixes that embed an IPv4 address, and Azure's platform address 168.63.129.16, which is public in form and internal in fact.

Parameters

allowedNetworks IEnumerable<IPNetwork>

Networks allowed even though the defaults deny them — an internal backend a deployment trusts. Checked before the denied list, so keep it as narrow as the need.

Networks denied on top of the defaults.

Remarks

An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address (::ffff:127.0.0.1) is judged as the IPv4 address it carries, which is where the socket ends up.

IsHostAllowed(string)

Whether a host name may be looked up at all. Names that can only mean "inside" — localhost and the internal suffixes — are refused without asking DNS.

public Task<IPAddress[]> ResolveAllowedAsync(string host, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)

Parameters

host string
cancellationToken CancellationToken

Returns

Task<IPAddress[]>

Remarks

Any denied address refuses the whole name, not just that address. A name answering with one public and one private address is either misconfigured or an attempt to win a race, and neither is worth connecting to.
